stops.name: Yangzhou, three years' governance
stops.campa: The Khan sets Marco to govern the great city of Yangzhou for three years, one of twenty-seven cities under its jurisdiction, so the canon claims, though later scholars find no Chinese record of a foreign governor by that name in these years and guess at some lesser office dressed up in the telling. True governor or trusted officer of the Khan's revenue, Marco walks streets of silk-weavers and salt-merchants that a memorial hall to him stands in today, the one Chinese city that claims him for its own civic memory rather than merely a place he passed through.

stops.name: Karajang (Yunnan), the mission to the western marches
stops.campa: Sent far southwest into Karajang, the province the Chinese call Yunnan, Marco crosses country of tigers and gold panned from riverbeds and cowrie shells passing for small coin, and describes with a naturalist's frankness the black-toothed, tattoo-legged people of Zardandan and the strange custom by which a new father takes to his bed forty days while his wife rises at once to nurse both him and the newborn child. It is the farthest south the canon sends him, on the edge of Burma and the elephant-kingdoms, before the road turns him back toward the capital and, eventually, toward the sea.
stops.quote: In this country gold-dust is found in great quantities; that is to say in the rivers and lakes, whilst in the mountains gold is also found in pieces of larger size... And for small change they use porcelain shells.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. XLVIII-XLIX (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Quinsai (Hangzhou), the city of heaven
stops.campa: Of every city the canon names, Quinsai (Hangzhou), capital once of the fallen Song, draws from Marco the longest and warmest chapter of all: a hundred miles around, twelve thousand bridges, some high enough for masted ships to pass beneath unstruck, a lake ringed with pleasure-boats and pavilions, ten great market squares thronged twice weekly, and streets so populous he will not set down the number for fear of being disbelieved. He calls it simply the greatest city in the world, and its name, which he renders 'city of heaven,' seems to him no exaggeration at all.
stops.quote: The city is beyond dispute the finest and the noblest in the world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. LXXVI (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Zaiton (Quanzhou), the port of ships beyond counting
stops.campa: Zaiton, the great port of Manzi, is where Marco reckons the pepper trade of the whole world passes a hundredfold what reaches Alexandria for the Christian markets, an exaggeration, perhaps, but the harbor he describes is real enough: a forest of masts, junks loading porcelain and silk for India and the Arabian Sea, merchants of every nation come to buy and sell. He will return to this same port in a few years' time not as a trader but as an escort, when the Khan at last agrees to let the three Venetians go home by the only road that will still take them: the open sea.
stops.quote: It is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II, ch. LXXXII (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Zaiton, departure with the Lady Kökötchin
stops.campa: An embassy from Arghun Khan of Persia asks Kublai for a bride of his own Mongol line; the choice falls on the young princess Kökötchin, and the overland roads west lie too torn by war for a bride's slow procession. The three Polos, homesick after two decades and lately fallen from favor with rivals at court, beg to escort her by sea and carry the Khan's leave to go home after. Thirteen four-masted ships with twelve sails apiece and six hundred souls put out from Zaiton in spring, the largest single fact of the whole return voyage, and Kublai's last great gift to the men who served him so long.
stops.quote: He then caused thirteen ships to be equipt, each of which had four masts, and often spread twelve sails.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue, ch. XVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Champa, the kingdom of pepper and elephants
stops.campa: The fleet coasts down past Champa, a rich kingdom of its own king and tongue, tributary to the Great Khan since Marco's own earlier embassy years helped settle the terms, he claims, though the chronology strains to fit. Elephants and lign-aloes wood are its wealth, and a court custom Marco records with plain wonder: that the king keeps three hundred and twenty-six wives and children beyond counting, and that no beautiful woman in the realm may marry until the king has had the first offer of her, a right he does not always take, but always holds by law.

stops.name: Sumatra (Ferlec), five months waiting out the monsoon
stops.campa: The contrary monsoon pins the fleet five months at anchor off the island the canon calls Java the Less, Sumatra, long enough that Marco builds a stockaded camp ashore against the wilder tribes of the interior, whom he describes, not without relish, as eaters of their own kind's flesh and worshippers of whatever creature first crosses their path each morning. He counts eight separate kingdoms on the one island, each with its own king and tongue, and the strange fixed stars of a sky already tilting toward a hemisphere he has never before sailed under in his whole life.
stops.quote: They dug large ditches on the landward side to encompass the party, resting at either end on the sea-haven, and within these ditches they made bulwarks or stockades of timber for fear of those brutes of man-eaters.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book III, ch. X (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Ceylon, the isle of gems and Adam's Peak
stops.campa: Ceylon, smaller than its old fame but for Marco still the finest island of its size on earth, yields rubies, sapphires, topazes, and amethysts washed from its rivers, and a mountain the natives say holds the tomb of our first father Adam, which the Saracens venerate as much as the idolaters, a rare moment where Marco records three faiths reverencing the very same summit without contradiction troubling any of them. He prices a ruby he has seen at the local king's court beyond any gem the Great Khan himself possesses, high praise from a man who has stood inside Kublai's own treasury.
stops.quote: It has a compass of 2400 miles... You must know that rubies are found in this Island and in no other country in the world but this. They find there also sapphires and topazes and amethysts, and many other stones of price.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book III, ch. XIV (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Malabar coast, pepper, pearls, and the naked kings
stops.campa: Along the Malabar coast (Kayal's pearl-fishery, the pepper groves, the diamond and ginger markets), Marco catalogues kingdom after kingdom with the same close attention he gave the courts of Cathay: kings who go bare-chested and hung with jewels rather than robed, brahmins who will not kill so much as a fly, widows who leap living onto their husbands' pyres out of what the canon takes plainly as love and honor rather than compulsion. It is the last long coast before the strait to Persia, and the richest single stretch of ordinary trade goods he has catalogued since leaving Cathay behind him.

stops.name: Hormuz: the princess delivered, the Khan Arghun dead
stops.campa: The fleet makes Hormuz at last with the princess Kökötchin still under the Polos' charge: six hundred souls sailed from Zaiton, a bare eight lived to see this harbor, so hard was the crossing, Marco says, though he and his own kin are all three still standing. Word meets them on the quay that Arghun Khan, for whom the bride was chosen, has been dead two years; his son Ghazan, campaigning on the frontier, will take her instead when he succeeds to the throne. The Polos hand her over to the regency and, their long charge discharged at last, turn overland for home.
stops.quote: When they embarked, they were in number some 600 persons, without counting the mariners; but nearly all died by the way, so that only eight survived.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue, ch. XVIII (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Trebizond and Constantinople, the last leg of the world
stops.campa: From Persia the Polos ride the last long overland stage through Tabriz once more, across Greater Armenia and down to the Black Sea coast at Trebizond, then by ship on to Constantinople, the city where Nicolò and Maffeo had begun their whole adventure thirty-four years before as young merchants of the Latin quarter. Byzantine officials, the family later complains, relieve them of a portion of their remaining wealth in customs and outright extortion before they can take ship again for the Adriatic, a last, small robbery after surviving the length of Asia not once but twice over.

stops.name: Venice: the return, unrecognized at their own door
stops.campa: Twenty-four years gone, the three Polos come home in coarse Tartar dress, their Venetian speech gone rusty and strange, and their own kinsmen at the Corte del Milione do not know them and bar the door. It is only, family tradition tells, when they slit the seams of their patched and shabby coats and let cascades of rubies, sapphires, and pearls spill across the table that the household believes: these ragged Tartars are indeed Nicolò, Maffeo, and Marco Polo, richer than the doge, and the whole city that had given them up for dead spends the following days feasting the men it once mourned.
